sections.html:
Gloucester occupies the lower Middle Peninsula between the York River, on its southern edge, and the Chesapeake Bay. Gloucester Courthouse is the seat. U.S. 17 crosses the York on the George P. Coleman Memorial Bridge toward York County, and Richmond lies roughly 60 miles to the west.

Population stood at 38,711 in 2020 and is estimated at 40,097 for 2025. The county has 17,049 housing units, 9.2% of them vacant in 2020, and owners live in 79.8% of the occupied ones. About 24 percent of its 288 square miles is water, leaving 218 of land, so flooding and insurance are routine questions from buyers.

For 2026 the county charges $0.583 for each $100 of assessed value. Property is valued at 100 percent of fair market value and revisited every three years, with a 2026 reassessment and a 2023 reassessment both in the county's document list. New construction gets listed and appraised between cycles, using building permits.

Values come from the Department of Real Estate Assessment at 6489 Main Street, Suite 126, phone 804-693-1325. Its appraisers work by mass appraisal, reacting to sales and market shifts instead of setting market values themselves. Billing and collection belong to the Treasurer, at 804-693-2141.

InstallmentDue dateWhat happens if unpaid
First halfJune 3010 percent penalty from July 1, plus 10 percent annual interest
Second halfDecember 5 (December 7 in 2026)Penalty after the due date

First-installment bills are mailed in early June and second-installment bills in early November. This year the December due date slides to December 7 since the 5th lands on a weekend. Paying the full year by June 30 is allowed. If a mortgage company escrows your tax, the duty to see it paid still rests with you, so check that it went through. An e-billing portal for paperless statements is described on the Treasurer's page.

An administrative review at the Real Estate Assessment office comes first. The owner or an authorized agent submits the county's application before the deadline printed on the reassessment notice. Most disputes are resolved right there.

Still unhappy? Apply to the Board of Equalization, five citizens appointed by the Circuit Court. Skipping the review and going directly to the board is permitted, although most differences get settled in the department. A petition to the Circuit Court is the final step, and the Clerk can be reached at 804-693-2502.

At any level, bring recent comparable sales, photos of defects and a list of facts the assessor got wrong.

sections.h2: Relief for elderly and disabled owners
sections.html: The Commissioner of the Revenue, at 804-693-3451, handles elderly and disabled tax relief. The application window runs from February 1 to May 1. Ask about eligibility before it opens and file early so any question gets answered ahead of the deadline. If you plan to sell in the coming year, let the Commissioner and the title company know, so everyone sees the same record of what relief is on the house.

The Treasurer publishes delinquent lists. Real estate with tax owing for more than two years as of December 31 can be sold at public auction under the Virginia Code's bill in equity process, and the county names Taxing Authority Consulting Services, P.C. as a firm handling that work. An owner who sees a parcel on a list should call the Treasurer without delay, because a balance that old narrows your choices quickly. A normal sale before that point lets the closing agent pay the debt out of your proceeds, and you keep control of the price and the timing.

Virginia law puts the real estate tax lien first in line until the taxing authority is paid, with penalties and interest folded in. The closing agent takes the balance from your proceeds. Request a payoff from the Treasurer before you sign a contract, and request another near settlement should the date drift past an installment.

  1. Dig out the last bill and note the parcel number.
  2. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff that counts penalty and interest.
  3. Send the figure and the deed names to the title company.
  4. Once settlement is over, confirm the parcel shows paid in the Treasurer's records.

sections.h2: How a Gloucester sale lines up with the tax calendar
sections.html:
Think about the two installment dates when you pick a listing window. A closing soon after June 30 or December 5 tends to follow a fresh payment, and the payoff stays simple. A closing mid-cycle calls for a proration, and the contract should assign the months before and after closing day.

If a due date is about to pass while the house is under contract, ask the Treasurer whether paying now or at settlement is cleaner. Treat any bill already mailed as live until the Treasurer says otherwise. An escrow account changes none of this, since unpaid tax comes out of the sale no matter who was supposed to pay it.

sections.h2: What to prepare for a cash offer
sections.html:
Even a buyer who takes a house as is needs the paperwork in order. Put these in one folder:

  • The latest tax bill and the parcel number.
  • Any reassessment notice or appeal paperwork.
  • The deed, or the estate papers if the owner has died.
  • Records of septic, well, roof and drainage work.

With that folder ready, an offer, a payoff and a closing date can come together fast. When the owner has died, the personal representative's authority must be documented before anyone signs a deed, so begin that step early.

Water shapes the market here. Many parcels lie near tidal creeks, marsh or river frontage, and a buyer's inspector will look at water-related points first. Expect those questions early and have your answers and receipts ready.

  • Check for moisture in crawl spaces and under porches on low lots.
  • Find out how old the septic system and the well are on rural parcels.
  • Keep receipts for roof or drainage repairs, because a buyer will ask for them.

Inherited land may come with old deeds that cite parishes and landmarks long gone. The Circuit Court clerk can pull the chain of title, and the sooner you ask the less likely the deed is to stall a sale.

Owners here often hold inherited waterfront or rural land, older homes that need repairs, or houses where tax slipped past the June 30 or December 5 dates. A cash sale avoids showings, repair bids and waiting on a buyer's loan. Cash Home Buyers purchases Gloucester County houses as they are, and the title company clears unpaid real estate tax from the proceeds at closing. Set a written payoff beside any offer to see what stays with you, and compare it with the cost of repairs and a long listing.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 real estate tax rate in Gloucester County?
faqs.a: $0.583 per $100 of assessed value for 2026. Real estate is assessed at 100 percent of market value.

faqs.q: When are Gloucester County real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: June 30 and December 5, with the December date moved to December 7 in 2026 because the 5th falls on a weekend.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for paying late in Gloucester County?
faqs.a: The county adds a 10 percent penalty after the due date and charges 10 percent annual interest on what stays unpaid.

faqs.q: How often does Gloucester County reassess real estate?
faqs.a: Every three years. The county lists reassessment documents for 2023 and 2026.

faqs.q: Where do I file a Gloucester County assessment appeal?
faqs.a: Start with an administrative review at the Real Estate Assessment office, then the Board of Equalization, then the Circuit Court. The reassessment notice shows the deadlines.
